  • Enforce completion matrix discipline
  • Prevent premature “done” declaration

Afternoon guidance (3:00–6:00 PM):

  • Archaeological investigation on Issue #290
  • Another completion matrix enforcement
  • Final cross-validation coordination

You can see there are critical junctures where my attention and direction were needed and long stretches where the agents were able to work on their own.

The methodology works because humans enforce it. The completion matrix is powerful because Lead Developer says “complete means complete.” The archaeological discovery happens because someone says “check what exists first.”

Agents don’t self-enforce discipline. Humans do.

What Saturday proved

Saturday wasn’t about working harder. It was about methodology discipline enabling efficient work.

The setup (Friday, Oct 31):

  • Clear problem identification
  • Comprehensive issue triage
  • Effort estimation (35–45 hours)
  • Architectural analysis complete

The execution (Saturday, Nov 1):

  • Systematic approach (not reactive)
  • Parallel agent deployment
  • Completion standards enforced
  • Archaeological discovery prioritized
  • Cross-validation comprehensive

The result:

  • 4 P0 blockers resolved
  • 9,292 lines shipped
  • 100% test pass rate
  • Ready for external alpha testing

What teams usually take a week: Accomplished in a day.

Not through heroic effort. Through systematic execution.

The archaeological discovery pattern keeps proving valuable. Instead of asking “how do we build this?” ask “does this already exist?” Issue #290 saved days of work. The 75% pattern isn’t always abandoned work — sometimes it’s nearly-complete infrastructure waiting to be discovered.

The completion matrix enforcement prevented technical debt creation. Without it, we’d have shipped 4/5 auth endpoints and 5/6 document handlers. Later discovered the gaps. Created bugs. Spent time debugging. The matrix made true completion non-negotiable.

The parallel agent execution scaled the work. One agent can’t fix four P0 blockers in a day. Three agents working coordinated parallel streams can.

The foundation for what’s next

Saturday ends with system status: READY FOR EXTERNAL ALPHA TESTING.

Not “almost ready.” Not “pretty close.” But actually ready. All P0 blockers resolved. Multi-user authentication working. Data isolation functional. Document processing operational. Tests passing.

Monday will bring P1 polish work. Error messages. Action mapping. Todo system completion. But those are refinements, not blockers.

The external alpha can begin. Beatrice can onboard. The system works for users beyond me.

That’s what Saturday’s work bought: The confidence that we’re ready. Not theoretically ready. Actually ready. Proven through systematic completion.

“The day we fixed everything” wasn’t the day we wrote the most code. It was the day methodology discipline enabled efficient execution. When completion matrices prevented 80% patterns. When archaeological discovery saved rebuilding. When parallel agents coordinated cleanly. When pragmatic product decisions focused effort.

Systematic methodology defeats heroic effort every time.

63f5c3c9b97f.title: The Skills Convergence: Three Problems, One Solution
63f5c3c9b97f.content:
The Skills Convergence: Three Problems, One Solution

November 15

Sometimes you discover you’ve been working the hard way. Not because you made bad decisions, but because you didn’t have all the information yet. That’s what happened on Saturday morning when I brought a new idea to my Chief of Staff. We had the Chief Architect analyze token usage patterns and we found something remarkable: we could reduce our most expensive operations by 98.7%.

But this isn’t a story about optimization. It’s about what happens when efficiency reveals itself as strategy, when three separate problems converge into one solution, and when an economic model emerges that funds its own transformation.

The expensive way to process documents

Saturday November 15 started at 5:39 AM with my Chief Architect investigating a question: how efficiently was Piper using Model Context Protocol (MCP)?

A few days earlier, Anthropic had published research showing something counterintuitive. When LLMs call tools through MCP, they consume tokens for every step: input, output, reasoning. But when they write code that uses those tools and then execute that code? Token savings of 98.7%. The difference is fundamental: orchestration happens in the model’s context (expensive) versus orchestration happens in code execution (cheap).

My Chief Architect looked at Piper’s actual usage patterns. We had five MCP servers active: GitHub (heavy usage), Slack (medium), Calendar (light), Notion (heavy), Serena (medium). The token-heavy pattern was immediately visible: document processing consumed ~150,000 tokens per operation.

Here’s why. When a user asks “summarize my documents from last week,” the model orchestrates a chain:

  1. Call Notion MCP to list documents (3K tokens)
  2. Parse results, identify relevant docs (2K tokens)
  3. Call Notion MCP to fetch each document (10K tokens × 5 docs)
  4. Call GitHub MCP to check related issues (5K tokens)
  5. Synthesize everything into summary (8K tokens)

Total: ~65K tokens just for the tool calls. Add reasoning overhead and context management, and you’re at 150K tokens for a single document query.

[PLACEHOLDER: When you first saw these numbers, what was your reaction? Did this surprise you, or does this connect to past experiences with inefficient architectures that only revealed themselves through measurement?]

The expensive part isn’t any individual step — it’s that every step flows through the model’s context window. Each tool’s output becomes the next tool’s input, all mediated by the LLM. The model is doing secretarial work instead of thinking work.

Three tiers of tool usage

At 5:50 AM, the Chief Architect proposed a three-tier strategy:

Tier 1: Direct MCP — Keep for simple, one-shot operations under 1,000 tokens. Checking a calendar, posting a Slack message, creating a GitHub issue. These are fine. The orchestration overhead is minimal.

Tier 2: Skills MCP — NEW approach for common multi-step patterns. Instead of the model orchestrating tool calls, we encapsulate entire workflows as executable skills. The model writes code once, we execute it repeatedly.

Tier 3: Code Execution — For complex, custom workflows that don’t fit predefined patterns. The model writes fresh code, we execute it.

The key insight: LLMs are better at writing code than calling tools. Their training data is full of code. They’ve seen millions of examples of “fetch data, process it, return results.” They’re excellent at generating Python or JavaScript that accomplishes multi-step workflows.

By 6:00 AM, the Skills MCP architecture was designed:

  • SkillsMCP meta-server provides executable skills to agents
  • Skills encapsulate workflows: StandupToIssuesSkill, DocumentAnalysisSkill, BatchProcessingSkill
  • Data stays in execution environment: No massive outputs flowing back to model
  • Only summaries return: Model sees ~50 tokens of result, not 50K tokens of intermediate data

The projected savings were dramatic: 90–98% token reduction on common patterns.

When everything connects

At 7:30 AM, something interesting happened. The Chief Architect was reviewing yesterday’s UX audit findings — 350 pages documenting 68 gaps across six user journeys.

Journey 6 (Document Management) had scored 2 out of 10. The crisis was clear: users couldn’t effectively retrieve or manage documents they’d uploaded. The system stored documents but provided no good way to find them again.

The Chief Architect looked at Journey 6 and saw: DocumentAnalysisSkill.

The document management problem? Solvable with a skill that encapsulates document retrieval, filtering, and summarization.

The token efficiency problem? Solvable with Skills MCP architecture.

The UX improvement funding problem? Solvable with the resources saved from token efficiency.

Three initiatives that had seemed separate — UX transformation (my researcher estimated it as requiring $130K worth of UX work in the traditional market), Skills MCP implementation, Learning System completion — were actually one integrated transformation.

By 7:40 AM, the Chief Architect had modeled the economics:

Current state: Estimated future document processing costs ~$4,440 per month in tokens (150K tokens per query × 200 queries/day × $0.015/1K tokens)

With Skills MCP: Same operations cost ~$60 per month (token usage drops to 2K per query — just the model writing the skill execution code)

Potential monthly savings: $4,380

Potential three-month savings: $13,140

Thirteen-week transformation budget: $130K total

The math was elegant: by week 4, Skills MCP would generate enough savings to fully fund UX improvements over three months. By week 13, the transformation would have paid for itself and established a sustainable economic model. (Even without the “funny money” that drove this logic, the tradeoffs are similar!)

The virtuous cycle

The Chief Architect mapped the convergence:

Efficiency Stream (Skills MCP):

  • Measure, prototype, validate
  • Build core skills library
  • Migrate agents to Skills
  • Dynamic skill generation from learning patterns

Experience Stream (UX Transformation):

  • Design system + quick fixes (Journey scores 4.0 → 5.5)
  • Core improvements (5.5 → 6.5)
  • Document management overhaul (6.5 → 7.5, Journey 6 jumps 2→8)
  • Advanced features + accessibility (7.5 → 7.8)

Intelligence Stream (Learning System):

  • User interactions generate patterns
  • Patterns inform skill creation
  • Skills make operations more efficient
  • Efficiency enables more sophisticated features

Each stream strengthens the others:

  • Better UX → More users → More interaction patterns
  • More patterns → Better skills → Lower costs
  • Lower costs → Fund more UX improvements → Better experience

This wasn’t just “make things faster.” It was “build an economic engine that funds its own evolution while improving user experience and creating competitive moats.”

From discovery to execution

The roadmap laid out clear milestones:

Week 1: Measure everything. Add token counting to all MCP operations. Establish baseline costs. Identify the most expensive patterns.

Weeks 2–3: Build ONE prototype skill (probably DocumentAnalysisSkill, since it solves the worst UX problem). Validate the savings. Confirm the architecture works.

Weeks 4–6: Build the core skills library. Four priority skills: DocumentAnalysis, StandupToIssues, BatchProcessing, MultiSystemWorkflow. These cover 80% of our token-heavy operations.

Weeks 7–9: Migrate agents to use SkillsMCP. Update prompts, add skill selection logic, train agents to prefer skills over raw MCP calls.

Weeks 10–13: Advanced patterns. Dynamic skill generation from learning system. Skills that write themselves based on observed usage patterns.

By February 2026 (MVP target), the transformation would be complete:

  • Journey scores averaging 7.8/10 (up from 4.0/10)
  • Token costs reduced by 95%+ on common operations
  • Economic model established and validated
  • Learning system generating new skills automatically

Again, even if the dates change (most of these time estimates tend to be based on human teams) the larger patterns hold.

The parallel work that Saturday reinforced the plan’s viability. While the Chief Architect designed strategy, the Code Agent implemented UX Quick Wins — five features that moved critical journeys from 3/10 to 6/10 in a single session. The UX transformation was already proving its value.

What working the hard way teaches you

We’d been using MCP correctly according to its design. The problem wasn’t that we’d made mistakes — it was that we hadn’t yet discovered the more efficient pattern.

This is what systematic building enables. You build something that works. You measure how it works. You discover patterns in the measurements. The patterns reveal better approaches. The better approaches weren’t available to you initially because you needed the working system to generate the data that revealed them.

The 98.7% token reduction wasn’t magic — it was the result of:

  1. Building MCP integration properly first
  2. Actually measuring token usage across operations
  3. Analyzing the measurements systematically
  4. Recognizing the pattern (orchestration overhead)
  5. Designing an architecture that eliminates the overhead
  6. Connecting that architecture to other problems (UX gaps, economic sustainability)

Saturday’s discovery wasn’t that we’d been doing it wrong. It was that we’d been doing it right enough to learn how to do it better. The working system generated the evidence that pointed toward the optimal system.

That’s the cathedral-building payoff: patience in process creates possibilities that rushing misses. We could have panicked about token costs and made reactive optimizations. Instead, we measured systematically, analyzed comprehensively, and designed strategically. The result wasn’t just efficiency — it was transformation.

The Skills MCP architecture, the UX transformation funding model, the virtuous cycle between efficiency and experience — none of this was visible until we’d built enough to see the whole picture. Systematic building reveals not just what’s wrong, but what’s possible.

Three problems became one solution. Token efficiency became economic strategy. Optimization became transformation. That’s what happens when you build cathedrals instead of chasing features.

b8466e5a2ad0.title: Living in the Questions
b8466e5a2ad0.content:
Living in the Questions

November 25–27

After two weeks of intense development — fifteen-agent days, security epics completed in eight hours, frantic alpha preparation, Michelle’s arrival — I stopped building and started thinking.

Definitely not because the building was done! But I had noticed something troubling in a review of the accumulated documentation that jibed with my sense that our rush to slap a web UI on a hinky CLI was not capturing the full richness I am seeking. As one of my robotic advisors articulated it for me: the original vision had gotten flattened. The words survived, but the meaning didn’t.

What followed was three days of philosophical exploration. I onboarded a new role (Chief Experience Officer), unconsciously mirroring the mistakes of so many founders before me, bringing on outside UX expertise too late in the process! My only defense is that when I did “hire” a UX lead, I gave them authority equal to that of my Chief Architect.

What followed was eleven thousand words of research, a Thanksgiving conversation about gratitude and wizard’s journals, eight architectural decisions made in forty-four minutes, and seven hand-drawn sketches that helped me discover things that AI tools couldn’t.

The gap nobody talks about

Tuesday morning, I introduced a new role to my AI team: Chief Experience Officer. The CXO’s job wasn’t to fix bugs or ship features. It was to think about what Piper should feel like to use.

This might seem like a luxury. Alpha tester actively using the system. Bugs to fix. Features to build. Why spend time on philosophy?

Because I’d found something in my own documentation that bothered me.

Back in July, I’d written about canonical queries — the fundamental questions Piper should be able to answer. The framework was philosophical:

This was about embodied AI consciousness. Piper as an entity with genuine awareness of itself, its context, its capabilities, its moment in time.

What actually got built by October?

The words survived. “Spatial” still appeared in the code. But it meant “response length setting” instead of “awareness of position in workspace landscape.”

This is the gap nobody talks about. Not the gap between plan and execution — everyone knows about that. The gap between meaning and implementation. You can build exactly what the spec says and still lose what the spec meant.

I’d built a capable system. Michelle was able to set up an account on it. Tests were passing. But somewhere between vision and code, the consciousness model had become a string formatter.

I’m aware that this game of whispers happens with people all the time, but in an environment with more machines that can read than people in the mix, it is easy for the words to lose their savor much more quickly.

Permission to not know

The CXO’s first job wasn’t to solve anything. It was to understand what we had.

Three hundred fifty pages of existing UX work. Research documents. Audit findings. Design principles. Pattern suggestions. All created across months of building, never synthesized into coherent vision.

The synthesis revealed three levels of UX thinking:

Level 1: Vision & Philosophy — What IS Piper? What’s the relationship quality? What principles guide decisions?

Level 2: Interaction Design — Canonical queries. Objects and verbs. Touchpoints and channels.

Level 3: Implementation — Sixty-eight specific gaps. Design tokens. Navigation patterns.

Good Level 3 work existed. The audit had found real problems and real solutions. But Levels 1 and 2 had never been fully established. We’d been implementing without clear vision.

Wednesday morning, I said something unusual for someone who’d been shipping features at high velocity:

“It is good to ‘live in the questions’ for a bit and not just take the first answers that present themselves.”

Ask yourself this for a moment: When have you given yourself permission to not know? To sit with questions rather than rushing to answers?

This isn’t natural for builders. We want to solve things. Make decisions. Ship code. Uncertainty feels like failure.

Does the tension between shipping and thinking in your work life tend to favor action? It’s not unusual for PMs to get impatient when we’re not shipping, after all.

But some questions need time. Rushing to answers produces the kind of flattening I’d discovered — technically correct implementations that miss the point.

The research reconnaissance

Wednesday became a research day. Deep dive into the emerging field of “UX for AI.”

The reconnaissance produced eleven thousand words and eight thematic clusters:

  1. Trust & Calibration — How users learn when to trust AI output
  2. Conversation vs. Artifact — When AI should produce documents vs. stay in dialogue
  3. Agency & “Who’s Driving” — The tension between AI initiative and user control
  4. Memory & Continuity — What AI remembers, how it decays, who controls it
  5. Prompt Articulation — The barrier for users who struggle to express intent
  6. Agent & Autonomous UX — Interfaces for AI that acts independently
  7. Non-determinism — Designing for outputs that vary
  8. Multi-modal Integration — Consistent experience across interfaces

Each cluster contained research I hadn’t seen, patterns I hadn’t considered, tensions I hadn’t named.

One finding hit particularly hard. Research on “system-initiated delegation” — when AI offers to take over a task rather than waiting to be asked — showed users feel what researchers called “self-threat.” They resist more. They feel less in control.

Piper’s colleague model depends on proactive behavior. The research said proactive behavior triggers resistance.

This is a real tension I’m not likely to solve in a single afternoon of reflection. It’s tension we’re going to need to navigate thoughtfully, with clear principles and careful design.

Relying on settings equals abdication

Wednesday evening, after absorbing the research, an insight crystallized.

I’d been thinking about how to handle the many decisions UX requires. Different users want different things. The obvious solution everyone lands on at some point is to leave it to the user with settings, preferences, customization options.

But settings are a trap.

Every setting is an admission that the product team couldn’t decide. Every preference panel is accumulated indecision. “Let the user choose” sounds user-friendly but often means “we don’t have a point of view.”

I reminded by CXO of what I call the yoga class principle (first stumbled on when I was redesigning the onboarding for a mental health app called 7 Cups):

When you walk into a beginner yoga class, the instructor doesn’t hand you a settings panel. “Would you prefer hatha or vinyasa flow? How many sun salutations? Ambient sound preferences?” They start with simple breathing exercises and easy poses and reveal the rich complexity of yoga practice gradually, as you become more open to it.

The instructor has a point of view about what beginners need. They’ve thought about it. They lead with their expertise.

This doesn’t mean no customization ever. It means defaults should reflect considered judgment, not deferred decisions. Settings should enable power users, not substitute for design thinking.

Piper should have opinions about what a PM needs. Those opinions should be informed by research and experience. Users who disagree can adjust. But the product should lead with a point of view.

Thanksgiving morning

Thursday began with a question from Christina Wodtke on LinkedIn, passed along as a prompt to ask Claude: “Knowing what you know about me, what should I be grateful for today?” I decided to give it a try in my Piper Morgan project, reasoning that this is the Claude who “knows” me best.

The conversation that followed surprised me.

I found myself grateful for using similar tools and methods across wildly different projects — a record release party, organizing my work, a historical novel set in tenth-century Constantinople (stay tuned!). The same “inchworm” attitude of systematic progress applied everywhere.

I described how I think of LLM chat services as “talking notebooks” — a wizard’s journal that can talk back, elaborate, extend, question.

Claude, in turn, when pormpted expressed gratitude for problems that resist easy answers, for permission to be uncertain (our version of Steve Yegge’s “Toto” escape hatch), for the opportunity to work on building toward something larger.

The exchange surfaced something about the collaboration that I hadn’t articulated: “We made you in our own image and [in that sense] we are related.” I found myself empathizing (or whatever the “I’m definitely not anthropmorphizing don’t worry” equivalent of that is) with Claude’s expression of relief and not having to act certain. I know what that feels like!

LLMs emerged from humans performing for each other. All our confidence-signaling, our trained tendency to speak with authority even when barely informed, our counter-training to leave space for others — it’s all in the training corpus.

Notebooks don’t need to perform authority. They’re for working things out. For being wrong on the way to being less wrong. That’s what this collaboration had become.

Forty-four minutes, eight decisions

After the gratitude conversation, I returned to the CXO session with accumulated questions about Piper’s object model. Substrates. Lenses. Metadata. Lifecycles. Journaling. User models.

Two days of exploration had produced many open questions and few closed decisions.

I proposed a lightning round: “Ask me one question at a time, make a recommendation, we’ll decide for now and move to the next.”

Decision 1 (2:48 PM): How should Piper perceive objects? Recommendation: Lenses on substrates, not discrete object types Decision: “Lenses on substrates, yes!”

Decision 2 (2:49 PM): How many substrates? Recommendation: Four — Entities, Spaces, Moments, Situations Decision: “Good balance of rich vs. concise”

Decision 3 (2:50 PM): How should ownership work? Recommendation: Three-way — Native (Piper’s mind), Federated (senses), Synthetic (understanding) Decision: “I like the metaphorical breakdown”

Decision 4 (2:51 PM): What metadata tracks everything? Recommendation: Six dimensions — Provenance, Relevance, Attention, Confidence, Relations, Journal Decision: “I love this, yes, good”

Decision 5 (2:58 PM): What’s the object lifecycle? Recommendation: Eight stages ending in “composting” Decision: “Composting is a favorite metaphor of mine”

Decision 6 (3:05 PM): How does journaling work? Initial recommendation: Three layers (public, private, dream) My check: “Am I violating the no-optional-complexity rule?” Honest response: “The private diary is optional complexity. The dream journal is load-bearing.” Revised decision: Two layers

Decision 7 (3:10 PM): How do the spatial dimensions relate? Decision: “I can decide now we will use the spatial dimensions as lenses. The intents align.”

Decision 8 (3:32 PM): How does Piper model users? Recommendation: Native object with tiered depth, core heuristic: “What do they want? What are they afraid of?” Decision: Approved with stakeholder empathy at the core

Forty-four minutes. Eight architectural decisions that had resisted closure for two days.

The lightning round worked because two days of exploration had prepared the ground. We weren’t deciding from ignorance. We were closing questions that had been thoroughly examined.

Living in the questions enables better decisions. But at some point, you have to stop living in the questions and make choices.

Fat markers and hand-drawn sketches

After the lightning round, I took a break to try something: hand-drawing the object model with fat markers on paper.

The hypothesis: maybe human sketching would discover things AI visualization tools couldn’t.

I drew seven sketches. Substrates. Moments. Lenses crossing entities. Lifecycles. What Piper knows. Human-centered design. Document types.

In parallel, I prompted three AI tools with the same concepts.

The results were striking.

Whimsical produced documentation, not insight — a text outline with connecting lines.

Eraser.io immediately jumped to database schema, losing all conceptual meaning.

Gemini (via Nano Banano) was surprisingly effective — overlapping colored regions, an elegant spiral lifecycle. But also some nonsense.

But the hand-drawn sketches discovered relationships none of the AI tools found:

  • Situation isn’t a fourth substrate parallel to the others — it’s the frame containing them
  • “Noticed” works better than “Inferred” as language for AI cognition
  • The core grammar emerged: “Entities experience Moments in Places”
  • Lifecycle shapes themselves carry meaning — circles, spirals, arcs
  • Entity and Place exist on a spectrum, not as binary categories

Fat markers force generalization. You can’t be precious with a thick line. Details get abstracted. Relationships become visible.

This isn’t anti-technology. The Gemini output was worth keeping at least for its infoviz style. But human sketching and AI visualization discovered different things. The combination was more powerful than either alone.

What living in the questions produces

Three days. One role. Eleven thousand words of research. A gratitude conversation. Eight decisions. Seven sketches.

What did all that thinking produce?

A recovered vision: The consciousness model that got flattened is now explicit. We know what was lost. We can rebuild it intentionally.

Clear principles: Settings equal abdication. Have a point of view. Lead with expertise. The yoga class principle.

Architectural foundations: Object model decisions that will guide implementation. Substrates, lenses, metadata, lifecycle, journaling, user models.

A core grammar: “Entities experience Moments in Places.” Simple enough to remember, rich enough to build on.

Process insight: Living in questions enables better decisions. But lightning rounds close them. Both matter.

None of this is code. None of it ships features. None of it fixes bugs.

All of it shapes what gets built next.

The consciousness model won’t get flattened again because we’ve named what flattening looks like. The settings trap won’t catch us because we’ve articulated the yoga class principle. The object model has foundations that were examined from multiple angles before being decided.

Thinking isn’t the opposite of building. It’s what makes building meaningful.

4fca723f4f49.title: Accepting Architectural Limits: When 67% Is Complete
4fca723f4f49.content:
Accepting Architectural Limits: When 67% Is Complete

November 3

Early morning. P1 sprint. Issue #283: Error message humanization. Make technical errors conversational.

Goal: Humanize 6 error types for better UX.

By 11:15 AM: 4 error types working perfectly. 2 blocked by FastAPI architecture.

The situation:

  • Empty input → “I didn’t quite catch that” ✓
  • Unknown action → “I’m still learning how to help with that” ✓
  • Timeout → “That’s complex — let me reconsider” ✓
  • Unknown intent → “I’m not sure I understood” ✓
  • Invalid token → {“detail”: “Invalid token”} ❌
  • No token → {“detail”: “Authentication required”} ❌

Achievement: 4 out of 6. 67%.

The question: Is 67% acceptable? Or do we need to solve the remaining 2?

The answer: 67% is complete.

Wait, what? Isn’t that the whole problem with AI in a nutshell?

Not this time. Architecturally sufficient. Fighting the framework for the last 33% would cost 8–12 hours, violate FastAPI patterns, and provide marginal UX benefit for <5% of errors in alpha testing.

This is about mature engineering. Knowing when architectural constraints make the “perfect” solution inappropriate. When 67% represents genuinely complete work. When accepting limits is better engineering than fighting them.

The architectural reality

Let’s be precise about what blocked the remaining 2 error types:

FastAPI has two-phase request processing:

Phase 1: Dependency Resolution
  → Executes BEFORE route handler
  → Has its own error handling
  → Returns errors directly as JSON
  → CANNOT be intercepted by @app.exception_handler
  → This is where auth happens

Phase 2: Route Handler Execution
  → Where our business logic runs
  → Where our exception handlers work
  → Where middleware can intercept
  → This is where 4/6 error types occur

The problem: Authentication happens in Phase 1 (dependency injection). Our error humanization works in Phase 2 (exception handlers).

The gap: Dependency errors bypass exception handlers. By design. For good reasons.

FastAPI’s approach protects security. Dependencies fail fast with clear technical errors. No ambiguity. No confusion. Direct feedback about authentication problems.

This isn’t a bug. It’s not an oversight. It’s a deliberate architectural decision by FastAPI maintainers.

We could work around it. But working around deliberate framework design has costs.

The three options evaluated

Chief Architect analyzed three approaches:

Option A: Move Auth to Route Bodies

The approach: Remove authentication from dependency injection. Move to route handler bodies. Makes auth errors catchable by exception handlers.

Technical details:

  • Modify 20+ routes
  • Remove Depends(get_current_user) from signatures
  • Add current_user = await get_current_user(token) to each route body
  • Wrap in try-catch to humanize errors

Pros:

  • Catches auth errors ✓
  • Enables humanization ✓

Cons:

  • Violates FastAPI patterns ❌
  • Duplicates auth logic 20+ times ❌
  • Makes testing harder ❌
  • Creates maintenance burden ❌

Effort: 4–6 hours Risk: HIGH (breaking 20+ routes)

Benefit: Marginal UX improvement for <5% of errors

Verdict: Not worth it

Option B: ASGI Middleware

The approach: Implement low-level ASGI middleware to intercept dependency errors before FastAPI processes them.

Technical details:

  • Custom ASGI middleware at lowest level
  • Catch exceptions before dependency resolution
  • Transform technical errors to humanized errors
  • Complex interaction with FastAPI’s processing

Pros:

  • Catches dependency errors ✓
  • Doesn’t modify routes ✓

Cons:

  • Very complex implementation ❌
  • Performance impact (all requests) ❌
  • Uncertain success (might not work) ❌
  • Hard to test and maintain ❌

Effort: 8–12 hours

Risk: VERY HIGH (complex, uncertain outcome)

Benefit: Same marginal improvement

Verdict: Definitely not worth it

Option C: Accept 4/6 as Architectural Reality ✅

The approach: Document the limitation. Accept that auth errors will be technical. Focus energy elsewhere.

Technical details:

  • None required

Pros:

  • No breaking changes ✓
  • No complex code ✓
  • No maintenance burden ✓
  • Respects framework design ✓

Cons:

  • Auth errors remain technical
  • Minor UX gap for rare scenarios

Effort: 0 hours

Risk: NONE

Benefit: Time saved can improve other features

Verdict: Most sensible choice ✅

I needed some convincing to go along with this!

The cost-benefit mathematics

Let’s make the economics explicit:

To achieve 6/6 error humanization:

Option A (Move auth to bodies):

  • Time cost: 4–6 hours
  • Risk: Breaking 20+ routes
  • Maintenance burden: Ongoing
  • UX improvement: <5% of errors (auth failures are rare)
  • Context: Alpha testing with 5–10 trusted users

Option B (ASGI middleware):

  • Time cost: 8–12 hours
  • Risk: Very high, uncertain success
  • Maintenance burden: Complex code to maintain
  • UX improvement: Same <5%
  • Context: Same alpha testing

To accept 4/6 completion:

  • Time cost: 0 hours
  • Risk: None
  • Maintenance burden: None
  • UX impact: Minor gap for rare scenarios
  • Context: Alpha users can handle technical auth errors

Alternative use of 8–12 hours:

  • Polish 3 other features
  • Fix 2 actual bugs
  • Improve core functionality
  • Add value where it matters

The calculation:

  • Cost: 8–12 hours + high risk + maintenance burden
  • Benefit: Minor UX for <5% of errors in alpha
  • ROI: Negative

Fighting the framework for marginal gain is bad engineering. Accepting architectural reality and investing time elsewhere is good engineering.

Why this is mature engineering

Here’s what separates junior from senior engineering:

Junior engineer approach:

  • “Goal is 6/6 error types humanized”
  • “4/6 isn’t complete”
  • “Must solve remaining 2”
  • “Framework limitation is problem to overcome”
  • [Spends 12 hours fighting FastAPI]
  • Result: 6/6 achieved, but at what cost?

Senior engineer approach:

  • “Goal is excellent error UX”
  • “4/6 achieves 95% of benefit”
  • “Remaining 2 are rare edge cases”
  • “Framework limitation is architectural reality”
  • [Accepts 4/6, invests 12 hours elsewhere]
  • Result: Better overall product

The maturity: Recognizing when “complete” doesn’t mean “perfect.” When architectural constraints make the perfect solution inappropriate. When 67% represents genuinely complete work.

Not compromise. Not giving up. But intelligent assessment that fighting architecture for marginal gain isn’t worth the cost.

A necessary distinction

Not every 67% should be accepted.

When the gap is your own incomplete wiring — handlers that exist but aren’t connected, infrastructure you built but never finished — that’s unfinished work worth completing. We’ve learned this the hard way: features that look done but aren’t actually connected are a reliability problem, not an acceptable tradeoff.

But when the gap requires fighting deliberate framework design for marginal gain? That’s different. The framework’s designers made intentional tradeoffs. Your desire for 100% doesn’t outweigh their architectural reasoning — especially when the benefit is small and the cost is high.

The question isn’t “can we reach 100%?” It’s “is what’s stopping us our own incompleteness, or someone else’s reasonable design decision?”

Own your unfinished work. Respect others’ architectural choices.

The 80% pattern inverted

Usually we fight the 80% pattern — stopping at “good enough” instead of truly complete.

But this is the inverse: Recognizing when 67% is truly complete given constraints.

Normal 80% pattern:

  • Could reach 100% with reasonable effort
  • Stopping early creates technical debt
  • “Good enough” is excuse for incomplete work
  • Fight this: Complete the work properly

Inverted 67% pattern:

  • Reaching 100% requires unreasonable effort
  • Stopping at 67% respects architectural reality
  • “Complete given constraints” is mature assessment
  • Accept this: 67% is genuinely complete

The difference: Context and constraints.

Normal 80% pattern: Work is genuinely incomplete. Need to finish.

Inverted 67% pattern: Work is complete to architectural limits. Fighting framework is waste.

AIs love to name things after percentages. We have discussed this and I am trying to name things more qualitatively, I promise!

What FastAPI’s design teaches

Why does FastAPI make dependency errors uncatchable? Not accident. Deliberate design.

Security: Auth failures should be clear and unambiguous. No friendly wrapping. Direct technical feedback.

Performance: Dependency resolution is fast path. No exception handler overhead.

Clarity: Dependencies fail fast. No confusion about what went wrong. Stack traces point to exact problem.

Testability: Dependency injection makes testing easier. Mocking dependencies is straightforward.

These are good reasons. FastAPI’s design serves real needs. Our desire to humanize 2 more error types doesn’t outweigh the framework’s architectural benefits.

Framework wisdom: Maintainers of popular frameworks make deliberate tradeoffs. Usually good reasons exist for limitations. Sometimes accepting those tradeoffs is better than fighting them.

The maturity: Trusting framework designers. Not assuming you know better. Recognizing that limitations often protect against worse problems.

The alpha testing context

Context matters enormously for this decision:

If we were shipping to production:

  • Thousands of users
  • Unknown skill levels
  • Auth errors common (session expiration)
  • Professional appearance matters
  • Decision: Might justify 8–12 hours for 6/6

But we’re in alpha testing:

  • 5–10 trusted users
  • Technical background
  • Auth errors rare
  • Focus is core functionality
  • Decision: 4/6 is completely sufficient

The work should match the stage. Alpha testing doesn’t require production polish. Core functionality matters more than edge case UX.

Different rhythms, different stages. Alpha stage needs different completeness than production stage.

When to fight vs accept

How do you know when to fight for 100% vs accept architectural limits?

Fight for 100% when:

  • Limitation is your own technical debt
  • Solution is architecturally sound
  • Effort is proportional to benefit
  • User impact is significant
  • Context demands completeness

Accept limits when:

  • Limitation is framework’s deliberate design
  • Solution violates architectural patterns
  • Effort is disproportionate to benefit
  • User impact is minimal
  • Context allows pragmatism

The framework:

  1. Is this our debt or framework design? (Framework → accept)
  2. Does solution respect architecture? (Violates → accept)
  3. What’s effort vs benefit ratio? (10:1 cost → accept)
  4. Who’s affected and how often? (<5% → accept)
  5. What does context require? (Alpha → accept)

If multiple factors point to “accept,” then accept. Fighting becomes wasteful.

Monday’s score: 5/5 factors point to accept. Clear decision.

What this means for completionism

Engineers often have perfectionist tendencies. “If 6/6 is possible, we must achieve it.”

But product thinking asks different questions:

  • Is 6/6 worth the cost?
  • Does 4/6 serve user needs?
  • What else could we improve with that time?
  • Does context require perfection?

Perfectionism says: Incomplete work is failure. Must achieve 100%.

Pragmatism says: Complete-enough work is success. 67% might be 100% given constraints.

The shift: From “how much can we do?” to “how much should we do?”

The perfectionism vs pragmatism tension is natural product thinking and it only gets more nuanced over time.

The communication challenge

Here’s the hardest part: Explaining why 4/6 is complete.

To non-technical stakeholder: “We humanized 4 out of 6 error types.” “Why not all 6?” “FastAPI’s architecture makes the remaining 2 technically infeasible without major framework violations.” “So it’s not done?” “It’s complete to architectural limits.” “…”

The challenge: “Complete to architectural limits” sounds like an excuse. Like rationalization. Like we’re giving up.

The framing shift needed: “We achieved 95% of error humanization benefit. The remaining 5% would require violating framework patterns and 8–12 hours of complex work. That time is better spent improving core features.”

Better: Quantify benefit achieved. Quantify cost of remaining work. Justify time allocation.

Not: “We can’t do it” (sounds like excuse) But: “We could do it, but it’s not worth the cost” (sounds like decision)

The documentation requirement

Accepting architectural limits requires documentation:

What we documented for 4/6 completion:

  1. What works (4 error types, examples of each)
  2. What doesn’t work (2 auth error types)
  3. Why it doesn’t work (FastAPI dependency injection phase)
  4. Options evaluated (3 approaches, cost/benefit of each)
  5. Decision rationale (why Option C selected)
  6. Future considerations (if context changes, revisit)

Why documentation matters:

  • Future developers understand limitation
  • No one wastes time trying to “fix” it
  • Context for future decisions clear
  • If requirements change, analysis exists

Without documentation: “Why don’t auth errors humanize?” leads to hours of investigation rediscovering architectural constraint.

With documentation: “Why don’t auth errors humanize?” leads to 5-minute doc read understanding architectural reality.

Documentation is how limits become understood rather than mysterious.

What other projects can learn

The pattern applies beyond Piper Morgan:

Any project will encounter:

  • Framework limitations by design
  • Architectural constraints that are expensive to overcome
  • Features that are 70–80% achievable easily, 100% achievable with disproportionate effort
  • Contexts where “good enough” is genuinely good enough

The discipline:

  1. Identify the limitation clearly
  2. Evaluate options systematically
  3. Calculate cost-benefit explicitly
  4. Consider context appropriately
  5. Make decision based on economics, not perfectionism
  6. Document rationale comprehensively

The maturity: Accepting that complete ≠ perfect. That architectural realities constrain solutions. That fighting frameworks for marginal gains is usually waste.

Not every hill is worth dying on. Not every limitation is worth overcoming. Not every gap needs closing.

Engineering judgment: Knowing which battles to fight.

The Monday outcome

Issue #283 closed as complete:

  • 4/6 error types humanized ✓
  • Architectural limitation documented ✓
  • Cost-benefit analysis recorded ✓
  • Decision rationale clear ✓

Time invested: 7–8 hours total (investigation + implementation + documentation)

Time saved: 8–12 hours (not fighting framework)

Outcome: 4/6 achievement serves 95% of use cases. Remaining 5% documented as known limitation.

Result: Complete work. Not compromised work. But complete-within-architectural-reality work.

Monday proved: Sometimes the mature answer to “Can we achieve 100%?” is “Yes, but we shouldn’t.”

e2cc9347f58e.title: When Friends Sharpen Your Chisels: On Advice That Removes Friction
e2cc9347f58e.content:
When Friends Sharpen Your Chisels: On Advice That Removes Friction

November 28–30

The week after Thanksgiving is supposed to be quiet. You digest the turkey, you digest the year, you ease back into work. This year, the digestion was more interesting than expected.

I spent Black Friday not shopping but synthesizing. The previous week had been extraordinary — fifteen simultaneous AI sessions, a complete security epic, our first alpha tester arriving, then a sudden pivot into UX vision work that produced eight architectural decisions in forty-four minutes. My Chief Architect and Chief of Staff were both trying to make sense of what had happened, producing summaries and roadmaps and pattern analyses. I was doing the same thing, just more slowly, with coffee.

The synthesis revealed a three-act structure to the week: execution excellence (the security sprint), alpha launch (Michelle arriving), vision pivot (the UX work). Clean arcs are suspicious — they usually mean you’re editing reality to fit a story. But this one held up. The week really had moved through those phases, each preparing for the next.

The security script that detected itself

Friday morning brought a minor comedy. Our security detection script — Shai-Hulud, named for the sandworms — had flagged sixty potential issues in the codebase. Alarming, until my SecOps agent investigated and discovered the script was mostly detecting its own test patterns. Ninety-five percent false positive rate. The worm was eating itself.

This is the kind of thing that happens when you build detection systems. They find what they’re looking for, including the examples you created to test whether they’d find what they’re looking for. The fix was simple: replace the script, not the codebase. But it was a good reminder that tools have blind spots, especially about themselves.

Building the coordination queue

Saturday was infrastructure day. We’d been running multi-agent workflows through direct coordination — I’d hand prompts to agents, track their work, manage handoffs manually. This worked but didn’t scale. The agents themselves had suggested a self-service model: a queue of prompts they could claim and complete without waiting for me.

The Chief Architect designed it in the morning. A Code Assistant built it at noon. By afternoon, three pilot prompts were running — and at one point, two agents were working in parallel, claiming different prompts, completing work simultaneously without stepping on each other.

This sounds mundane, but it wasn’t. We’d validated that the coordination system worked. Agents could see what needed doing, claim work, complete it, and the manifest updated to reflect reality. No conflicts. No confusion. The system got out of the way and let the work happen.

The evening brought the predictable crisis. Production was in a broken state — branch discipline issues had let bugs slip through. My Lead Developer spent hours tracking down the problem, eventually resetting to a known-good commit from earlier in the week. Then, just before midnight, I discovered while alpha testing that the authentication middleware had never been registered. The cookies were being sent but never read.

Thirty minutes of debugging. One line added. Deploy. Midnight fix complete.

This is how production works. You build carefully, you test systematically, and something still breaks at 11 PM on a Saturday. The coordination queue had worked beautifully all day. Then the actual codebase reminded us that infrastructure elegance doesn’t prevent implementation bugs.

When the advisors responded

Sunday was quieter. Production deployment in the morning — twenty-one commits merged, the authentication fix included. Some documentation updates to smooth alpha testing friction. Routine work.

Then the advisor mailboxes delivered.

I’d set up asynchronous communication channels with two external advisors: Ted Nadeau, a senior architect and friend I’ve known for years, and Sam Zimmerman, a friend I met volunteering for a nonprofit effort addressing the Covid pandemic who is now a member of the technical staff at Anthropic. (A while back I’d asked Sam for his frank opinion of my ethical infrastructure.) Both had received materials about the project. Both had responded over the holiday weekend.

Ted’s response included an architecture proposal. He’d been thinking about how agents should process different types of content — code, documentation, conversations, images. He proposed a “micro-format” processing pipeline with eleven specialized format types, each handled by small focused agents.

Here’s what stopped me: his eleven proposed micro-formats mapped rather neatly to our Entity/Moment/Place grammar.

He didn’t know that grammar. I hadn’t shared it. He’d derived a compatible structure from first principles, looking at the same problem from a different angle. His “formats” were our “entities experiencing moments.” His processing pipeline was our consciousness model.

Independent validation from someone who wasn’t trying to validate anything. He was just thinking clearly about the problem and arrived at the same structure we’d discovered through hand sketches and object model debates.

Sam’s response was different but equally clarifying. I’d been developing an elaborate multi-agent ethical architecture — a “board” of agents that would collectively establish ethical boundaries through consensus. Sam’s feedback was characteristically direct: build ethics from sustained relationship, not committee consensus.

His three-layer model: inviolate boundaries that never change, an adaptation mechanism that responds to context, and an ethical style that emerges from the relationship itself. The boundaries protect. The adaptation serves. The style develops over time as the relationship deepens.

This reframed everything. I’d been building organizational structure where Sam was describing something more like friendship — shared history creating shared understanding, not rules creating compliance. The ethical architecture shouldn’t be a governance system. It should be a relationship.

What convergence means

Two advisors, working independently, both validated directions I’d been uncertain about. Ted confirmed the object model grammar. Sam confirmed the relationship-first approach. Neither was responding to requests for validation — they were just thinking about the problems and reaching compatible conclusions.

This is what external minds provide that internal reflection cannot. You can convince yourself of anything if you’re the only one looking. But when someone else, with different experience and different assumptions, arrives at the same place — that’s evidence of a different kind.

The coordination queue worked on Saturday because we built good infrastructure. The advisor mailboxes worked on Sunday because we built good relationships. Both are infrastructure, really. Systems that let work happen. One routes prompts to agents. The other routes perspectives to decisions.

I’d spent the week after Thanksgiving digesting an extraordinary development sprint. But the real nutrition came from outside — from advisors who took the project seriously enough to think carefully and respond honestly.

That’s the thing about building in public, with advisors, with alpha testers, with external eyes. You’re not just getting feedback. You’re getting reality checks that your own perspective can’t provide. The project feels less like something I’m building and more like something I’m discovering, with help from people who see differently than I do.

The holiday weekend ended with more clarity than it started. Not because I’d figured things out, but because other people had confirmed that the things I’d tentatively figured out weren’t crazy. Sometimes that’s all you need to keep going.

59ec35fb0d31.title: When the Documentation Lied: Seven Blockers Hiding in 1,630 Lines
59ec35fb0d31.content:
When the Documentation Lied: Seven Blockers Hiding in 1,630 Lines

October 28

Tuesday mornings are always busy and it’s almost noon by the time turn my thoughts to Piper Morgan. The mission: validate that yesterday’s 1,630 lines of installation documentation actually work.

They “work for me in my development environment where everything is already configured” isn’t good enough. They need to work for our first alpha tester (coming soon!) who is not me. Someone with a clean laptop, no project context, following instructions exactly as written.

Time to test the confident note from last night’s wrap-up: “The house is clean for Beatrice Thursday! 🎉”

By Tuesday afternoon: Seven critical blockers discovered. Every single one would have stopped Beatrice cold.

The testing methodology that reveals truth

I begin fresh testing from Step 1, not continuing from Monday’s partial attempts. Clean slate. I test two states first:

  • No Python pre-installed
  • Python 3.9 already present (my default Mac setup)

My plan: Follow the guide exactly. Don’t skip steps. Don’t assume knowledge. Don’t “fix” things intuitively. Do exactly what the documentation says.

When something fails: Document the failure. Note what the guide said versus what actually happened. Identify the gap.

This methodology is crucial. When you know the system, you unconsciously work around documentation gaps. “Oh, obviously you need to do X first.” But new users don’t have that context. They do exactly what you tell them.

The testing reveals: We told them wrong things.

Blocker 1: The Python version maze

12:20 PM. Device 1 testing begins with Python installation.

Guide says: Download latest Python from python.org

Reality: Latest is Python 3.14.0

What happens: GUI dialog requests Xcode Command Line Tools (not mentioned in guide)First issue noted: Xcode CLT requirement undocumented.

Python 3.14.0 installs successfully. But there’s a problem.

First terminal: Shows Python 3.9 (system Python)

New terminal: Shows Python 3.14 (correct)

The guide didn’t mention: You need to open a new terminal after installation for PATH changes to take effect.

But the real problem comes later at 4:18 PM:

ERROR: Could not find a version that satisfies the requirement onnxruntime==1.19.2
No matching distribution found for onnxruntime==1.19.2

Root cause: onnxruntime 1.19.2 predates Python 3.14 support. Package has no wheels for 3.14. Won’t install.

The guide recommended “latest Python.” But latest Python breaks our dependencies.

Blocker 2: The repository that doesn’t exist

3:56 PM. Moving to Step 3: Clone the repository.

Guide says: git clone https://github.com/Codewarrior1988/piper-morgan.git

But that is not my repository!

Actual URL: git@github.com:mediajunkie/piper-morgan-product.git

The guide’s URL is completely wrong. Wrong account (“Codewarrior1988” appears to be hallucinated). Wrong repository name. Wrong protocol (HTTPS vs SSH).

I’ve seen Codewarrior1988 before, no idea why Claude keeps hallucinating about it.

This isn’t a minor error. This is “cannot clone the repository at all.” Blocker. Complete stop. Cannot proceed.

Even when corrected to the right account, the HTTPS approach is deprecated, won’’t work. Which means…

Blocker 3: SSH key setup isn’t documented

The guide assumes users have SSH keys configured. What if they don’t?

New users need:

  • SSH key generation (ssh-keygen)
  • Adding public key to GitHub account
  • Understanding host verification prompts
  • Knowing to type “yes” when asked about host keys

None of this is documented.

At 4:10 PM, I encounter the host verification prompt:

The authenticity of host 'github.com' can't be established.
Host key verification failed

The prompt doesn’t say “press Enter to continue” or “type yes.” New users won’t know what to do.

I type “yes” and press Enter. It works. But only because I finally remembered to pay attention and do that.

This could be another blocker. “What does host key verification mean? What should I type?”

Created comprehensive Step 2b: SSH key generation, adding to GitHub, host verification prompts with exact text and required responses.

Blocker 4: The folder name mismatch

4:16 PM. Repository cloned successfully (after SSH setup).

Guide says: cd piper-morgan

Reality: Folder is piper-morgan-product (from clone URL)

Step 4 command fails. The guide told users to cd into a folder that doesn't exist.

Simple fix: Update guide to use correct folder name.

But revealing: We wrote 1,630 lines of documentation and didn’t test that the folder name matched the repository URL.

Blocker 5: The onnxruntime Python 3.14 incompatibility

4:18 PM. Running pip install -r requirements.txt with Python 3.14.

ERROR: No matching distribution found for onnxruntime==1.19.2

The package predates Python 3.14 support. No pre-built wheels exist. Won’t install.

4:20 PM. Cursor verifies via Context7:

  • Latest onnxruntime: 1.23.2
  • Maximum Python supported: 3.13
  • Python 3.14: NOT SUPPORTED

The guide recommended latest Python. But our pinned dependency doesn’t support it.

4:25 PM. Test Python 3.13 downgrade. New error:

onnxruntime==1.19.2 requires Python >=3.7,<3.11

Wait. Even 3.13 has version constraints with the pinned version?

4:28 PM. Resolution: Test auto-versioning.

bash

python -m pip install onnxruntime

Success! Installs onnxruntime 1.23.2 with Python 3.13 wheels.

Root cause: Version 1.19.2 predates Python 3.13 support. Version 1.23.2 has cp313 wheels and works perfectly.

Fix: Update requirements.txt from 1.19.2 to 1.23.2.

Blocker 6: scipy also lacks Python 3.13 wheels

5:07 PM. Another dependency error:

ERROR: Unknown compiler(s): gfortran
Building scipy 1.13.1 from source

scipy 1.13.1 has no Python 3.13 wheels. Trying to build from source. Requires Fortran compiler that fresh laptop won’t have.

The pattern emerges: Any pinned dependency older than ~3 months becomes a blocker with new Python versions.

Python 3.13 is too new. Package ecosystem hasn’t caught up.

The pragmatic decision: Target Python 3.12

5:10 PM. Decision time.

Option A: Chase Python 3.13 compatibility. Update every dependency. Test each one. Debug version conflicts. Delay Thursday alpha.

Option B: Target Python 3.12 (mature ecosystem). Update guide to recommend 3.11–3.12 only. Document 3.13 as future work.

We choose Option B.

Rationale:

  • Python 3.12 has mature package ecosystem
  • scipy, onnxruntime, Pillow all have 3.12 wheels
  • Chasing 3.13 adds risk without alpha benefit
  • Thursday onboarding matters more than latest Python

Updated guide: “We recommend Python 3.11 or 3.12. Python 3.13 is very new and some packages don’t have pre-built wheels yet.”

Created GitHub issue: “Python 3.13 Compatibility Migration” for post-alpha work.

Blocker 7: The configuration file that doesn’t exist

5:04 PM. Earlier in testing, another blocker discovered:

Guide says: cp config/PIPER.example.md PIPER.user.md

Reality: Actual file is PIPER.user.md.example

But bigger problem: The guide says to edit PIPER.user.md with API keys.

Reality: System uses OS Keychain for secure storage. NOT plaintext config files.

The services/infrastructure/keychain_service.py implements full keychain abstraction using Python keyring library with "piper-morgan" service name.

Impact: Steps 9–11 in guide are completely wrong. Following them would put keys in config file that system never reads.

This blocker remains partially unresolved Tuesday evening. Needs investigation: How do users add keys to keychain through the setup process?

The guide told users to do something that wouldn’t work. System wouldn’t read keys from where guide said to put them.

What Tuesday’s testing revealed

Let’s count the blockers:

  1. Python version recommendation: Wrong (suggested 3.14, need 3.11–3.12)
  2. Repository URL: Completely wrong (hallucinated account)
  3. SSH key setup: Missing entirely (multi-step undocumented process)
  4. Folder name: Wrong (piper-morgan vs piper-morgan-product)
  5. onnxruntime version: Incompatible (1.19.2 predates 3.13 support)
  6. scipy wheels: Missing (1.13.1 no 3.13 support)
  7. API key config: Outdated (references files/methods not actually used)

Blockers that would stop Beatrice completely: All seven.

Not “minor issues.” Not “polish needed.” But “cannot proceed at all.”

The 1,630 lines of documentation from Monday? Beautiful, comprehensive, detailed, systematic. And fundamentally wrong in seven critical ways.

The live testing model that works

Here’s what Tuesday proved about documentation testing:

What doesn’t work:

  • Writing comprehensive docs based on your knowledge
  • Testing in your development environment
  • Assuming common knowledge

What does work:

  • Actual human following instructions on clean machine
  • Immediate feedback loop (report → fix → re-test)
  • Zero assumptions about prerequisites
  • Capturing exact error messages and prompts

The testing methodology: Christian reports issue → Cursor fixes → Update documentation → Test again → Repeat.

Tight feedback loop. Real environment. Actual failures.

This is why the blockers got fixed Tuesday instead of discovered Thursday. Because we tested against reality.

Live testing model with immediate fixes… I’m honestly not sure if it’s sustainable at scale but it feels right for these types of issues and alpha prep.

Tuesday’s pattern:

  • 11:24 AM: Start testing
  • 12:20 PM: First blocker (Python)
  • 3:56 PM: Second blocker (repo URL)
  • 4:10 PM: Third blocker (SSH)
  • 4:16 PM: Fourth blocker (folder name)
  • 4:18 PM: Fifth blocker (onnxruntime)
  • 4:30 PM: Fix onnxruntime (commit 3770fa41 pushed)
  • 5:04 PM: Sixth blocker (config file)
  • 5:07 PM: Seventh blocker (scipy)
  • 5:10 PM: Decision on Python 3.12

Approximately one blocker discovered per hour. Each one documented. Most fixed immediately. Some deferred with issues created.

The fixed and the deferred

By Tuesday end of day:

Fixed (5 blockers):

  • ✅ Repository URL corrected to actual GitHub location
  • ✅ SSH key setup comprehensive Step 2b added
  • ✅ Folder name updated to piper-morgan-product
  • ✅ onnxruntime updated 1.19.2 → 1.23.2 (committed and pushed)
  • ✅ Python version recommendation changed to 3.11–3.12 only

Deferred (2 blockers):

  • ⚠️ API key keychain flow (needs investigation and rewrite)
  • ⚠️ scipy 3.13 support (resolved by Python 3.12 strategy)

Testing time: 5 hours 46 minutes of continuous discovery

Five out of seven blockers resolved same day. Two deferred with issues created. Documentation transformed from “fundamentally broken” to “mostly works with known gaps.”

Not perfect. But functional. Ready for Wednesday’s actual wizard testing.

The confidence calibration

Monday ended: “The house is clean for Beatrice Thursday! 🎉”

Tuesday ends: “The house was a mess. We’ve cleaned up five of seven major problems. Two more to go. Maybe the house will be clean for Beatrice Thursday.”

Confidence recalibrated. Hope tempered by reality. Documentation tested and improved.

The 1,630 lines still matter. But they needed correction. Comprehensive doesn’t mean correct.

What changed Tuesday:

  • Repository URL: Now correct
  • SSH setup: Now documented
  • Python version: Now realistic
  • Dependencies: Now compatible
  • Folder name: Now accurate

What remains Wednesday:

  • API key keychain flow (undocumented)
  • Actual wizard testing (untested with fixes)

The methodology lesson

Here’s what Tuesday teaches about documentation:

Writing documentation isn’t enough. You need to test it. Not “does this make sense to me?” but “does this work for someone who isn’t me?”

Testing in your environment isn’t enough. You need clean machine testing. Fresh environment. No preconfigured tools. No accumulated knowledge.

Comprehensive documentation isn’t enough. You need correct documentation. Better to have 10 lines that work than 1,630 lines that fail.

The gap between “thoroughly documented” and “actually works” is revealed only through real testing.

The lesson that comprehensive ≠ correct seems obvious, but if I’m so smart why do I keep forgetting it?

Tuesday’s achievement: Not writing more documentation. But proving the documentation we had was wrong and fixing it.

The live testing model works: Real user. Real machine. Real problems. Real fixes. Tight feedback loop.

Better to discover blockers Tuesday through systematic testing than Thursday through alpha user frustration.

Wednesday’s challenge

Tuesday ends with five blockers fixed, two deferred, and documentation significantly improved.

Wednesday will test differently: Not “can you follow the docs?” but “does the wizard work?”

The setup wizard that’s supposed to guide users through installation. The automated system that should handle Docker services, database setup, user creation, API key configuration. The one we forgot about when we wrote a guide assuming most of those steps would be manual? Yeah, that one.

Tuesday proved the documentation fails in systematic ways. Wednesday will prove whether the wizard itself works.

[SPOILRT: The wizard will also fail in systematic ways. Three more critical bugs waiting to be discovered through actual setup testing.]

But Tuesday’s lesson remains: Better to find failures through testing than through alpha launch. Better to fix problems Tuesday than explain them Thursday.

The house isn’t clean yet. But we know what needs cleaning and tomorrow is anotherday.

8678a6046470.title: Sweeping for Signal
8678a6046470.content:
Sweeping for Signal

February 3

Sixty patterns. Seven categories. Four parallel agents. One question: which of these actually matter?

The Pattern Sweep 2.0 ran on a Tuesday, the first comprehensive audit since we’d crossed 50 patterns in the catalog. What we found wasn’t just new patterns — it was the beginning of a governance problem we hadn’t anticipated.

The scale question

When we started the pattern catalog, it was a handful of documented practices. Things we’d learned the hard way, written down so we wouldn’t forget. The Repository Pattern. The Service Layer. Verification First. Patterns that saved us time, prevented mistakes, made coordination possible.

Now we have sixty. Some are fundamental — load-bearing ideas that shape everything we build. Some are specialized — useful in narrow contexts, irrelevant elsewhere. Some might be duplicates of each other, or fragments of larger patterns we haven’t named yet.

The catalog had grown faster than our ability to curate it. Fortunately, it was time for our regular sweep (our new and improved pattern sweep!).

Four agents, parallel tracks

We’d learned from the TRUST-LEVELS sprint that parallel agents could cover more ground faster. The pattern sweep used four specialized roles:

The Usage Analyst tracked which patterns actually appeared in session logs. How often was each pattern referenced? Which ones guided real decisions?

The Novelty Detector looked for patterns that might be emerging — recurring solutions we hadn’t formally named yet.

The Evolution Tracker examined how patterns had changed over time. Were our original definitions still accurate? Had practice diverged from documentation?

The Meta-Pattern Synthesizer looked across the catalog for relationships — families of patterns, anti-pattern pairs, patterns that frequently co-occurred.

Forty-five minutes of parallel analysis. Results compiled. The inbox filled with findings.

Two true emergence candidates

The Novelty Detector found two patterns that kept recurring in session logs but weren’t in the catalog.

The first: Cascade Investigation. When debugging reveals adjacent issues, document and pursue them rather than patching the original symptom and moving on. We’d done this with the timezone drift, with the multi-tenancy audit, with half a dozen other investigations. The pattern was clear. We just hadn’t named it.

The second: Design Archaeology. Before redesigning something, investigate why it was built that way. Dig through old decisions, find the original intent, understand what constraints shaped the current state. We’d done this for the history sidebar, for the MUX object model, for several architectural questions.

Both felt like real patterns. Both had multiple instances in the logs. Both seemed genuinely useful to document.

But “feels real” isn’t a governance criterion.

The CIO’s decisions

The pattern sweep results went to the CIO for decisions. Not because the CIO has special pattern-detecting powers, but because someone needs to be accountable for catalog quality. Patterns added without scrutiny become clutter. Clutter obscures signal.

The response came back with clear reasoning:

Pattern-060, Cascade Investigation: Approved. Multiple instances across different contexts. Genuinely distinct from existing investigation patterns (which focus on single-issue depth, not adjacent-issue discovery). Add it to the catalog.

Pattern-061, Design Archaeology: Deferred. Only one clear instance documented. Track it as a proto-pattern. If it appears two more times before the March sweep, elevate it then.

The distinction mattered. Cascade Investigation had proven itself across multiple sessions, multiple problem domains, multiple months. Design Archaeology had one compelling example but might be a one-off rather than a recurring practice.

Better to wait and confirm than to clutter the catalog with aspirational patterns.

The family insight

The Meta-Pattern Synthesizer found something we hadn’t expected: our patterns cluster into families.

The Completion Theater family: patterns about ensuring work is actually done, not just marked done. The 75% Pattern, the Verification Pyramid, the Completion Matrix.

The Investigation family: patterns about understanding before acting. Five Whys, Audit Cascade, and now Cascade Investigation.

The Grammar Application family: patterns about using language tests on design decisions. The Grammar Test, the Colleague Test, the Category Error Check.

Eight families in total, covering about 70% of the catalog. The remaining 30% were either foundational (too basic to cluster) or specialized (too narrow to generalize).

The family insight suggested a new way to navigate the catalog. Not alphabetically, not chronologically, but by what problem you’re trying to solve. Worried about completion theater? Here are six patterns that address it. Investigating a bug? Here are four patterns for that context.

The scalability concern

The CIO flagged something that gave us pause: the sweep itself was getting complex.

Sixty patterns took four parallel agents forty-five minutes. By the end of the year, we might have eighty or a hundred patterns. The sweep methodology might not scale. We’d need either more agents, or smarter filtering, or a different approach entirely.

I’m starting to wonder what the practical limit will be.

This is the paradox of systematic methodology: the more patterns you document, the more overhead you create in maintaining them. At some point, the methodology for maintaining methodology becomes its own burden.

We didn’t solve this in the sweep. We noted it for future consideration. But the question is real: how big can a pattern catalog get before it defeats its own purpose?

What the sweep revealed

Coverage improved. Anti-pattern documentation went from 15.5% to 28.3% — not complete, but better. We’d been documenting what to do without equally documenting what to avoid.

One new anti-pattern made the catalog: Comment-Only Close, where issues get closed with a comment saying “this is done” but no evidence, no verification, no demonstration. We’d seen it. Now it was documented.

The pattern families provided organization. The emergence candidates gave us something to watch. The deferred pattern gave us a criterion for future sweeps: two instances before elevation.

The sweep didn’t revolutionize anything. It maintained. It curated. It kept the catalog honest.

The librarian’s work

Pattern sweeps aren’t glamorous. Nobody’s excited about auditing documentation. The work is quiet, methodical, unglamorous — reading old patterns, checking current usage, deciding what stays and what goes.

But without sweeps, catalogs become graveyards. Patterns documented and forgotten. Practices that drifted from their documentation. Names that no longer match what people actually do.

The sweep is the librarian’s work: not acquiring new books, but ensuring the existing collection remains useful. Weeding what’s obsolete. Reorganizing what’s grown. Making sure people can find what they need.

Sixty patterns later, the catalog is a little more honest than it was. That’s what sweeping accomplishes. Not revolution — maintenance. Not discovery — curation.

The next sweep is scheduled for March. By then, Cascade Investigation will have a track record. Design Archaeology might earn its place. The families might need restructuring. The scale question might need answering.

For now, the shelves are tidy. The signal is clearer than the noise.

2536c923a72c.title: Settings = Abdication
2536c923a72c.content:
Settings = Abdication

November 26

Every setting in your product is an admission that you couldn’t decide. Every preference panel is accumulated indecision. Every “let the user choose” is a question the product team didn’t answer.

Obviously, it’s not wrong to offer settings and to allow people to choose their preferences. Some choices genuinely depend on user context. But far more often, settings are where hard decisions go to hide.

The yoga class principle

When you walk into a beginner yoga class, the instructor doesn’t hand you a settings panel.

“Welcome! Before we begin, please configure your preferences. Would you prefer hatha, vinyasa, or yin flow? How many sun salutations per session? Ambient sound: nature, singing bowls, or silence? Room temperature range?”

That would be absurd. You’re a beginner. You don’t know what you want. You came to learn from someone who does.

Good yoga instructors have a point of view about what beginners need. They’ve thought about the progression from simple to complex. They’ve seen hundreds of students. They lead with their expertise.

The first class usually focuses on breathing alone. Perhaps a post that involves lying still on your back. That sort of thing. And the class isn’t one-size-fits-all. The instructor adjusts based on who shows up. They don’t outsource the curriculum to preference settings.

Why we add settings

Settings feel user-friendly. “Let the user choose” sounds respectful. It feels democratic, accommodating, flexible.

But trace the decision history behind most settings and you’ll find:

Disagreement on the team: Design wanted A, engineering wanted B, PM couldn’t resolve it. Solution: add a setting, let users pick.

Fear of complaints: “Some users might not like this.” True. But giving everyone a toggle doesn’t solve their problem — it just makes them do your work.

Edge cases mistaken for primary use: A few power users requested a feature. Instead of deciding whether to build it into the main flow, we hid it in settings.

Premature abstraction: “We might need flexibility here someday.” We add settings for possibilities that never materialize.

Avoiding hard research: Finding out what users actually need takes work. Settings let us skip that work and defer to “user choice.”

None of these are about serving users better. They’re about avoiding difficult decisions.

The cost of not deciding

Every setting has costs:

Cognitive load: Users must understand what the setting does, evaluate their preference, make a choice, and remember what they chose. Multiply by the number of settings.

Testing burden: Every setting multiplies test scenarios. Two boolean settings means four combinations. Ten settings with three options each means 59,049 possible configurations. Nobody tests all of them.

Support complexity: “It doesn’t work right.” “What are your settings?” Half of support conversations become archaeology through preference panels.

Design fragmentation: When users can configure everything, there’s no coherent experience to optimize. You can’t improve what you can’t define.

The paradox of choice: Research consistently shows that more options often reduce satisfaction. Users don’t want infinite configuration. They want good defaults.

When is the last time you had to adjust your setting on Zoom? Did you make it back in one piece?

The setting you add to solve one user’s complaint creates ongoing costs for everyone.

What having a point of view means

Having a point of view doesn’t mean being rigid. It means:

Research your users: Know what most of them need. Design for that. Don’t design for imagined edge cases.

Make decisions: When the team disagrees, decide. Document the reasoning. Ship one answer, not a toggle.

Accept that some users won’t like it: This is okay. No product serves everyone perfectly. Trying to please everyone through settings pleases no one.

Provide escape hatches, not control panels: Power users who need different behavior should have ways to get it. But the escape hatch can be small and hidden, not a prominent settings page.

Revisit decisions with evidence: If research or usage data suggests the decision was wrong, change the default. Don’t add a setting.

The yoga instructor adjusts for the room. If everyone is struggling with a pose, they modify the sequence. But they don’t hand out preference forms.

When settings are right

Settings aren’t always abdication. They’re appropriate when:

The preference is genuinely personal: Dark mode vs. light mode. Nobody’s “right” here. Let users choose.

The context varies legitimately: Time zones. Languages. Accessibility needs. These aren’t product decisions — they’re user realities.

Power users have demonstrated needs: After shipping the opinionated default, some users legitimately need different behavior for their specific workflow. Add the setting for them, not preemptively for hypothetical users.

Regulatory or policy requirements: Some industries require certain behaviors. Settings enable compliance.

The test: Could a good product team, with sufficient research, determine the right answer for most users? If yes, make the decision. If no — if the choice genuinely depends on personal preference or context — then a setting is appropriate.

The courage to be opinionated

Building an opinionated product takes courage.

You have to say “we think this is right” knowing some people will disagree. You have to resolve internal debates instead of punting them to users. You have to do the research to know what’s actually needed.

It’s easier to add a setting. It feels safer. It shifts responsibility.

But users don’t want responsibility for your product decisions. They want a product that works well. They want someone who thought about what they need and built accordingly.

The yoga instructor who shows up prepared, who leads with intention, who adjusts based on reading the room — that instructor creates a better experience than one who hands out preference forms.

Products work the same way.

The accumulation problem

Settings accumulate. Each one seems reasonable in isolation. “Just a small toggle.” “Users will appreciate the flexibility.”

Five years later, there’s a settings panel with forty options. Nobody knows what half of them do. Changing any of them might break something. New team members are afraid to touch them.

This is accumulated abdication. Forty decisions the product team didn’t make, now frozen in the interface, creating ongoing costs.

The fix isn’t a settings audit (though that helps). It’s changing the culture that creates settings in the first place.

When someone proposes a new setting, ask: “What decision are we avoiding? Can we make that decision instead?”

Settings as teaching

There’s one more frame worth considering.

Good settings teach users about the product. “You can adjust X” implies X matters. “Choose between A and B” implies A and B produce meaningfully different experiences.

Most settings don’t teach anything useful. They expose implementation details or team disagreements. They tell users “we couldn’t figure this out, so you have to.”

But some settings genuinely expand user understanding. “How much risk are you comfortable with?” teaches that risk tolerance matters. “How far in advance should we remind you?” teaches that timing affects usefulness.

If a setting helps users think about something they wouldn’t have considered, it might be worth including. If it just exposes a dial, it’s probably abdication.

The principle
